rationale: I'm replacing the 5 coarse bands with the log relative spectrum in 1-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz on every channel. Abnormal clinical EEG is mostly about slowing, a lower or missing alpha peak and focal beta changes, and fixed band edges blur all three. The model has about 17× more features now, so I choose the regularization strength C with inner grouped CV on the training fold.

I'm changing Welch to take the median across segments instead of the mean (`average="median"`). These clinical recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few seconds of blinks, muscle bursts or electrode pops can inflate the mean power spectrum. The median of the 2-s segments should track the background rhythm better, and that rhythm (slowing, alpha loss) is what separates abnormal from normal EEG. It should also make the features more robust on external recordings with different artifact loads.

The relative spectrum is normalised per channel, so it discards amplitude. On clinical EEG, high-amplitude slowing, such as increased absolute delta/theta (often focal), is a hallmark of abnormal recordings. This change adds the log absolute power in 5 classical bands per channel, taken from the same median Welch PSD. The 1-Hz relative bins still describe spectral shape, and the new features restore the amplitude information. The same per-feature standardisation and inner-CV-tuned L2 logistic regression keep regularisation in check.

I'm adding per-band spatial covariance features. For delta, theta, alpha and beta, I band-pass the signal, average 2-s epoch covariances after dropping epochs with outlying power (robust MAD rule), and map each matrix to log-Euclidean tangent space (the upper triangle of its matrix log). The current features are per-channel spectra only, so they miss spatial structure. Focal slowing, interhemispheric asymmetry and changes in spatial coherence are classic signs of abnormal clinical EEG, and covariance matrices carry that information. Riemannian/tangent-space covariance features are among the strongest feature-based baselines on TUAB.

The median Welch spectrum and robust covariance averaging remove short events by design. Many abnormal clinical EEGs are abnormal precisely because of short events: intermittent (often focal) delta/theta slowing bursts and paroxysmal or sharp activity. This change adds the per-channel temporal variability of 2-s epoch power, using robust upper and lower quantile spreads of log relative power in 5 bands plus log total power, so the model can see those intermittent abnormalities.

I'm adding a LightGBM gradient-boosted tree model on the same features and blending its probabilities with the L2 logistic regression. The inner grouped CV picks both C and the blend weight. Clinical abnormality often depends on thresholds and interactions, such as focal slowing showing up only in some channels or bands, or slowing that matters only when the alpha peak is lost. A linear model can't represent those, and blending the two kinds of model is a well-established gain on feature-based TUAB work.

The model currently uses only spectral and covariance features. Spike, sharp-wave and other epileptiform transients are sharp, non-sinusoidal and heavy-tailed, so they barely change any spectrum, yet they are a main reason clinical EEGs get read as abnormal. This change adds per-channel time-domain shape features from 1–45 Hz band-passed 2-s epochs: median Hjorth mobility and complexity, the spread of mobility across epochs, median skewness, and median and 90th-percentile kurtosis.

This change adds hemispheric-asymmetry and focality features: the absolute difference in log band power (absolute and relative) between each homologous left–right channel pair, plus the largest positive and negative deviation of any channel from the across-channel median. Focal slowing or a one-sided loss of alpha is a classic abnormal finding, and it can appear on either hemisphere or at any electrode. That makes it a V-shaped function of the existing per-channel features, which the logistic regression cannot represent, and LightGBM, which samples 30% of columns per tree, has trouble finding it.

This adds explicit spectral-parameterization features per channel: the aperiodic 1/f exponent and offset, fitted in log-log over 2–40 Hz with the alpha range excluded, plus features of the 1/f-flattened spectrum at 0.25-Hz resolution. Those are the peak alpha frequency (argmax and centre of gravity), alpha peak height and area, and the size of any theta/delta bump. A slowed posterior dominant rhythm (below about 8 Hz) is a core criterion clinicians use to call an EEG abnormal, and peak position is an argmax/centroid that the linear model on 1-Hz relative bins cannot form, nor can LightGBM with 30% column sampling.

Clinicians judge the EEG background at the subject's most alert state, because slowing during drowsiness or light sleep is normal in routine recordings, while slowing that persists during wakefulness is abnormal. The current median spectrum over the whole 5 minutes mixes these states. This change picks the 2-s epochs with the least slowing (lowest 25% of the channel-median log (1–7 Hz)/(8–30 Hz) ratio), after dropping high-power artifact epochs. From those epochs it computes the per-channel relative spectrum and absolute band power. It also adds global quantiles of the slowing ratio over time, which describe how much of the recording is slowed.

I'm adding lagged phase-synchrony features. For each band (delta, theta, alpha, beta) I compute the weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) for every channel pair, using cross-spectra of 2-s Hann-windowed epochs after dropping high-power artifact epochs, and also each channel's mean wPLI (node strength). The covariance features only capture zero-lag coupling, which volume conduction dominates. wPLI picks up the true lagged interactions that encephalopathy, lesions and epileptiform networks disrupt, and it doesn't depend on amplitude scale, which should help on external amplifiers.

All ~2,700 heterogeneous features currently share one L2 penalty, so the ~760-dim covariance block and the ~930-dim spectral block crowd out small, dense blocks like spectral parameterization, focality and shape. This change fits a separate logistic regression per feature family, each with its own C picked by inner grouped CV. A meta logistic regression then stacks the out-of-fold logits from these block models, the full-feature logistic regression and LightGBM, so each physiological marker family gets the weight it deserves.

This adds a new family of features: per-channel nonlinear complexity and entropy. Each channel gets the median and 10–90% spread over 4-s epochs of the Higuchi fractal dimension, the median ordinal-pattern (permutation) entropy at two time scales (delay 1 and delay 4), and the spectral entropy of the median Welch spectrum. Diffuse encephalopathy and other abnormal backgrounds make EEG less irregular in ways that band power, Hjorth and covariance don't directly measure. These features don't depend on amplitude, so they should also hold up on external amplifiers.

The spatial covariance block gave by far the largest gain (+0.034), but it uses only 4 coarse bands. Clinically important distinctions happen inside those bands: slow 1–2 Hz vs 2–4 Hz polymorphic delta, posterior 6–8 Hz slowing vs normal 8–10 / 10–13 Hz posterior rhythm, low vs high beta (drug effects), and 30–45 Hz fast/muscle topography. So this change replaces the 4 bands with a finer 9-band filterbank for the log-Euclidean tangent-space covariances; the inner-CV-tuned L2 penalty keeps the extra features in check.

Right now each band covariance is projected with the log-Euclidean map at the identity, so the tangent features are dominated by the shared volume-conduction structure that every recording has. This change keeps the raw shrunk band covariances in `featurize`. Then, inside `fit_predict`, it computes a reference mean per band from the training fold only (no labels used) and maps each matrix to the tangent space at that mean, using the whitened log map logm(M^-1/2 C M^-1/2). This is the standard Riemannian tangent-space recipe that works well on TUAB, and the whitened features should show deviations from a typical recording, such as focal or diffuse slowing, more directly.

These clinical recordings have no artifact rejection, so some features have very heavy tails: kurtosis and skewness, tangent values from flat or saturated channels, and electrode pops. Under plain StandardScaler, a few extreme recordings can dominate the L2 logistic regression. This change scales each feature by its median and IQR, then soft-clips it with c·tanh(z/c), so outlier recordings carry less weight in the linear fit. It should also transfer better to external amplifiers. LightGBM, the features and the inner-CV selection of C and the blend weight are unchanged.

This round adds features computed on the TCP bipolar "double-banana" montage, the montage clinicians use when they read TUH recordings. Bipolar derivations emphasise local field gradients and cancel diffuse common activity, so focal slowing and focal sharp transients, which average referencing smears across the scalp, should show up more clearly. For each of up to 22 TCP derivations I add log absolute and relative band power from a median Welch spectrum, the across-epoch variability of band power, and waveform-shape features (Hjorth, skewness, kurtosis). The spatial covariance block is left alone because its tangent features already cover any fixed linear montage change.

This round adds an epoch-level classifier whose window scores are aggregated per recording. Abnormal findings such as intermittent focal slowing are often episodic and multivariate, so a subject-level median spectrum dilutes them. I store band power per 10-s window on both the average-reference and TCP bipolar montages, and fit a logistic regression on those windows. Its scores for each recording become extra features: mean, 10/50/75/90th percentiles, spread, and the fraction of windows scored abnormal. Training recordings get their scores out-of-fold from grouped CV inside the training fold, so their own labels never leak into their features.

Add pooled-region spectra. Clinicians judge diffuse background slowing and the posterior dominant rhythm over scalp regions, not single electrodes. Per-electrode spectra are noisy (local artifacts, bad contacts), and LightGBM cannot average across columns. For frontal, central, temporal, posterior and whole-scalp groups, I average the median-Welch PSD (0.25 Hz resolution) and extract the 1-Hz relative spectrum, log absolute band power and the 1/f + peak-alpha parameters. This should give low-noise markers of diffuse slowing and a more reliable posterior peak alpha frequency than the per-channel argmax.

This round adds a third model to the blend: an RBF-kernel SVM on the same robust-scaled, soft-clipped features. Abnormal recordings deviate from normal in many different ways (diffuse slowing, focal slowing, spikes, a missing alpha peak). A distance-based kernel can score how far a recording sits from the normal cluster, which a linear model or axis-aligned tree splits cannot express. The SVM's C, its Platt calibration and the three-way blend weights are all chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold. I haven't run it, so neither the Dev score nor the run time is known. My rough estimate is that the extra SVM fits add a few minutes to the CV.
